n: The plan of this lesson has six stages. First, on the basis of UN data and the concept of DRD, we consider the problem and classification. Then we study opiates, that is, opium, morphine and heroin. At the third stage we speak about cannabis and cocaine, that is, types of euphoria. The fourth is psychotropics: LSD, amphetamines and spices. The fifth stage covers dependence and sampling, precursors and laboratory issues. Finally we discuss changes in the body and the limit of a reliable conclusion.

t: Section 1: problem and classification, in brief
n: The first section is devoted to the problem and classification. This problem has medical, social and economic significance. Let us recall it through short questions. By effect, substances are divided into sedative and stimulant groups. By origin they are natural, semi-synthetic and synthetic. DRD means drug-related death. In our country cannabis and opiates occur. Among young people, amphetamines are on the increase.

Now we look at the number of users according to UN data. Users of cannabis preparations number 130–190 million people. Substances of the amphetamine group are taken by 30–40 million people. Users of heroin number 11.3 million, and of other opiates 4.1 million. Remember: these figures are taken from the textbook and the year is not stated. Therefore they cannot be tied to a specific year.

By character of action, substances are divided into two groups. The first is the sedative group: cannabis and opiates. With them euphoria proceeds with calm and relaxation. The second is the stimulant group: cocaine and amphetamines. With them euphoria is accompanied by psychomotor excitation and a psychostimulant effect is observed. That is, the type of euphoria differs according to the substance.

By origin, narcotic and psychotropic substances are of three kinds. Natural ones include cannabis, morphine, codeine and cocaine. Semi-synthetic ones are heroin, mescaline and ephedrone. Synthetic substances are exemplified by amphetamine, promedol, methadone and sombrevin. This classification shows how the substance is obtained.

Now let us consider distribution by region. Cannabis and opiates occur on the territory of our country. Cocaine is characteristic mainly of countries of the Western Hemisphere. Amphetamines are increasing in the world, especially among young people. Spices have been observed since the 2000s. That is, the place of distribution differs for each substance.

Drug-related death, in English Drug related death, abbreviated DRD. This includes cases of death directly or indirectly linked with a drug. These are: poisoning by a large dose, consequences of long-term use, suicide, accidents and death resulting from homicide. Thus DRD covers not only death from poisoning but also indirect cases.

Intoxication increases the likelihood of becoming a victim. It increases the risk of suicide, the risk of an accident and the risk of becoming a homicide victim. Examples of accidents: road traffic accident, fall from a height, burning in a fire and drowning. This means that a person under the influence of a drug more often gets into dangerous situations.

The second section is devoted to opiates. The source of opiates is the juice of the opium poppy. Its alkaloids are morphine, codeine, thebaine and narcotine. Heroin is a semi-synthetic substance, acetylated morphine. Opiates accumulate in large amounts in the liver. In the body they are detected for several months. Death from poisoning occurs from paralysis of the respiratory centre.

The toxicokinetics of opiates is as follows. When taken by mouth, absorption begins after 20–30 minutes, and with subcutaneous injection after 10–15 minutes. Opiates begin to be eliminated as soon as they are absorbed into the blood. They are present in all tissues, more in the liver. For morphine the liver-to-blood ratio is about 5-fold. Elimination is maximal in 8–12 hours, and in 3–4 days about 90 % has been eliminated.

Opiate poisoning lasts from several hours to a day. First nausea and vomiting appear. Then marked cyanosis is observed and the pupil constricts. After that dyspnoea and torpor develop. Finally coma begins, and death occurs from paralysis of the respiratory centre. Remember this sequence in order.

Let us consider the lethal doses of opiates. By mouth, dry opium 2–5 g. Morphine by mouth 0.2–0.4 g. Morphine by the parenteral route 0.1–0.2 g. That is, with parenteral administration the lethal dose is smaller than by mouth.

The third section compares cannabis and cocaine. The character of euphoria differs according to the substance. Cannabis is obtained from the plant Cannabis sativa, cocaine from the leaves of the coca bush. Cannabis is smoked or taken by mouth. Cocaine is taken through the nose, intravenously or subcutaneously. With cannabis there are calm and relaxation, with cocaine psychomotor excitation. In both the pupil dilates. Death from cannabis does not usually occur, whereas with cocaine death is from the respiratory centre and fibrillation.

Cannabis poisoning usually runs without death, because cannabis breaks down quickly. First the pupil dilates and nystagmus appears. Then tachycardia is observed and blood pressure rises. Then a brief psychosis begins. Finally weakness and sleep come.

In cocaine poisoning, death occurs from the respiratory centre or ventricular fibrillation. Poisoning begins with euphoria and psychomotor excitation. Then pulse and breathing quicken and blood pressure rises. After that arrhythmia and dyspnoea appear. In the last stage consciousness is disturbed.

The fourth section is devoted to psychotropics. In this group vegetative disturbance and disturbance of consciousness come together. Hallucinogens include LSD, psilocybin, phencyclidine and mescaline. Amphetamines are phenylethylamine derivatives, and MDMA is included among them. Spices are mixtures with synthetic cannabinoids.

Under the action of hallucinogens, vegetative and mental signs are observed together. In vegetative disturbance there are tachycardia, raised blood pressure and dilated pupils. In disturbance of consciousness there are misperception of reality, delirium and hallucinations. That is, the body and the consciousness are affected at the same time.

Amphetamines are synthetic derivatives of phenylethylamine. Their action is similar to cocaine, but weaker and longer. Amphetamines stimulate the central nervous system. They are taken mainly by mouth. They are distributed as club tablets, that is, party-pills. The substance called “ecstasy” is MDMA, whose lethal dose is 500 mg.

Under the action of amphetamines mood is raised, fatigue passes, and physical and mental activity increase. There are other signs too: appetite falls, sleep is lost, and tachycardia and profuse sweating are observed. Nausea, vomiting, a metallic taste in the mouth and diarrhoea also occur. In some cases poisoning may end in death.

Spice is translated from English as “seasoning”. Its composition is plant material and a synthetic cannabinoid. It is a mixture intended for smoking. Packets are 0.5–3.0 g. Compared with cannabis, spices act more strongly and for longer. Signs: tachycardia, trembling and convulsions.

t: Section 5: dependence and laboratory, in brief
n: The fifth section is devoted to questions of dependence and the laboratory. Repeated intake leads to habituation of the organism. Dependence is psychological and physical. If intake is stopped, a withdrawal syndrome appears. A precursor is a substance used in preparing a narcotic. For the laboratory, blood, urine, saliva and washings are taken. The period of detection in urine varies from hours to days, depending on the substance.

We distinguish the types of dependence. Psychological dependence is expressed by an irresistible urge to take the substance. In physical dependence tolerance appears and the need to increase the dose arises. Withdrawal is the development of a syndrome when intake is stopped. Do not mix up these three concepts.

Let us consider the textbook example on habituation to opiates. Habituation occurs in 25–30 days. The dose may reach 10.0 g per day. The withdrawal syndrome lasts 5–6 days. This example is given for opiates.

Doctors should know about precursors. The word precursor is from English precursor, meaning one that comes before. Precursors are substances used in preparing narcotics. Their list is approved, just like that of narcotics. Examples: hydrochloric and sulphuric acid, acetone and toluene. In addition ephedrine, ergotamine and piperidine are listed.

Samples are taken to detect cannabinoids. Materials are taken as quickly as possible. Blood 10 ml, urine 10 ml and saliva 10 ml are taken. In addition, a washing of the fingers of the hand is taken, for which alcohol-soaked cotton wool or gauze is used.

When cannabis smoking is suspected, a washing is taken. The first step is wiping: the fingers are wiped with alcohol-soaked cotton wool or a gauze swab. The second step is evaporation: the alcohol evaporates at room temperature. The third step is packaging: the swab is wrapped in a polyethylene bag. Carry out the procedure in this sequence.

Table 6.2 shows the detection periods of some substances in urine. Cannabinoids begin from 1–3 hours and are detected for 24–168 hours. Heroin begins from 2–6 hours and lasts 24–72 hours. Methamphetamine begins from 4–6 hours and is detected for 48–72 hours. Cocaine begins from 2–6 hours and lasts 48–72 hours. Phencyclidine begins from 4–6 hours and is detected for 7–14 days.

t: Section 6: changes in the body, in brief
n: The sixth section is devoted to changes in the body. These changes are conventionally divided into four groups. The first is specific changes, which are found only by complex laboratory methods. The second is signs of repeated intake, which depend on the route of entry. The third is infections spread by injection. The fourth is signs of lifestyle: emaciation, tattoos and others.

The first group is specific changes. They are of a neurochemical and neurophysiological nature. Such changes are determined only under experimental conditions. They are found within a very short time after death by neuro- and immunohistochemical methods. Therefore they are of no significance for forensic practice.

The second group is signs of repeated intake. The signs depend on the route of entry of the substance. With intravenous injection there are small ulcers and scars along the course of the veins. A non-sterile solution causes vasculitis and endocarditis. Abscesses and angiogenic sepsis are also possible, and granulomas appear in the lungs and liver. With intranasal intake, chronic inflammation of the nasal mucosa, aspiration pneumonia and granulomas in the lungs are observed. With oral intake, in cocaine and amphetamines, there is ischaemic damage of the intestine.

The third group is injection infections: AIDS and viral hepatitis. The fourth group is signs of lifestyle: emaciation, tuberculosis, venereal diseases, skin tattoos, that is, a syringe, a flower and a butterfly, pediculosis and inability to carry a pregnancy. Remember: none of these signs proves use.

Let us define the limit of the conclusion. Changes in the body have the character of indirect evidence, and therefore do not give a reliable, categorical conclusion. The circumstances of the incident are assessed together. Catamnesis and clinical picture are also assessed together. The forensic chemical result, however, is regarded as the main evidence.

t: Teaching case 1: signs in the body
n: The first teaching case. This is a hypothetical case, not a real examination. Given: small ulcers and scars along the veins, granulomas in the lungs and liver, emaciation and skin tattoos. There are three questions. Changes of which group are observed? Can use be stated categorically? What else is needed? Try to answer yourself.

The answer to the first case. These signs belong to group 2 and group 4. There is no categorical conclusion, because they are indirect evidence. The circumstances of the incident and the clinical picture are also needed. The decisive evidence is the forensic chemical results. The signs do not give a reliable conclusion.

The second teaching case is also hypothetical, not a real examination. Given: cannabis smoking is suspected, and the patient has been brought to hospital. Questions: which samples are taken? How is the washing taken? When is it taken? First think for yourself.

The answer to the second case. For cannabinoids, samples of 10 ml each are taken: blood, urine and saliva. For a washing, the fingers are wiped with alcohol-soaked cotton wool. Then the alcohol evaporates and the swab is packed in a polyethylene bag. Samples are taken as quickly as possible.

Let us gather the main points of support of the lesson. DRD includes direct and indirect death. In opiates, death is from paralysis of the respiratory centre, and they are detected for months. In cocaine and amphetamine, euphoria with excitation is observed. Dependence is psychological and physical, with withdrawal. Signs in the body are indirect, not categorical. A reliable conclusion rests on forensic chemistry and the circumstances of the incident.

The review questions rest on pp. 167–172 of the chapter. First question: what is “drug-related death”? Second: what are the toxicokinetics and lethal dose of opiates? Third: what is the clinical difference between cannabis and cocaine? Fourth: how do psychological and physical dependence differ? Fifth: list the four groups of changes in the body.
